explain.say: A puddle does not soak away completely; much of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapour and drifts into the air. This is evaporation.

explain.say: Water molecules are always jiggling at different speeds. At the surface, the fastest ones break free and escape into the air, and warmth from the sun makes more of them fast enough.

faq.a: Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface, below its boiling point. The fastest-moving molecules escape into the air.

faq.q: Why do puddles dry faster on windy days?
faq.a: Wind blows away the moist air just above the puddle and replaces it with drier air, so water molecules can keep escaping instead of falling back.
asks: Does wind make water evaporate faster?

faq.q: Does water need to boil to evaporate?
faq.a: No. Water evaporates at any temperature, even on cold days, just more slowly. Boiling is when vapour bubbles form all through the liquid, not just at the top.
asks: Can water evaporate when it's cold?

faq.q: Why do shallow, wide puddles dry fastest?
faq.a: Evaporation only happens at the surface. A wide, shallow puddle has lots of surface for its amount of water, so it dries much faster than a deep one.
asks: Does the shape of a puddle matter?

faq.a: It becomes water vapour, an invisible gas in the air. Later it can cool and condense into clouds and fall as rain, so the water is never lost.
asks: Where does evaporated water end up?

facts: Water vapour is invisible; the white mist above a kettle is tiny droplets that have already condensed.
Ice and snow can also turn straight into vapour without melting, which is called sublimation.
